title: Paint one cell and change a byte
audience: Students with basic programming knowledge who are new to assembly
learningObjectives: Distinguish an address from the value stored there
Pack RGB components into a word
Relate byte order to increasing memory addresses

quiz.prompt: How many logical cells does this header describe?

choices.text: 4096: every screen position is a separate memory word.
One: the assignment name changes the grid dimensions.
Four: two columns times two rows.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
The configuration describes two columns and two rows. Each logical cell occupies a 32 by 32 screen block. A future verified screenshot will show the exact editor and display arrangement.

completion.reason: The book supplies instruction checkpoints; native trainer automation is pending.

quiz.prompt: How far apart are these word addresses?

choices.text: Thirty-two bytes because a word has 32 bits.
Four bytes.
One byte because each is one word.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
pixel starts at 0x10010000 and neighbor starts at 0x10010004. Their values are initially 0 and 0x13579bdf. A declaration alone is not the runtime drawing operation taught here.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of $t0 here?

choices.text: To identify the destination memory location.
To hold the red component only.
To choose a syscall service.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
The address register identifies the first data word. No store has changed that word yet.

quiz.prompt: Which byte specifies blue in the packed word?

choices.text: 0x33 because it is the first nonzero pair written.
0x00 because the highest byte always specifies blue.
0x99, the least significant byte.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
The components are red 51, green 102, and blue 153. The color is in a register; the pixel word is still unchanged.

completion.reason: The book supplies instruction checkpoints; native trainer automation is pending.

quiz.prompt: When is the register color transferred into memory?

choices.text: When the assembler reads the label base_ready.
When sw executes.
When li loads the constant.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
The word at pixel is 0x00336699. In the configured grid, the upper-left cell should show that color. The neighboring word is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Which byte is at the lowest address in this lesson?

choices.text: 0x00 because it is written first in the hexadecimal word.
0x33 because red is the first color channel.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
In little-endian memory the bytes at offsets 0, 1, 2, and 3 are 99, 66, 33, and 00 in hexadecimal. The packed word remains 0x00336699.

quiz.prompt: How many bits will sb take from the source register?

choices.text: All 64 bits.
Exactly 24 bits because the display uses RGB.
Eight low bits.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
The low byte of $t2 is ff. The pixel has not changed merely because this register was loaded.

quiz.prompt: What is the final packed word?

choices.text: 0x000000ff because sb clears the rest of the word.
0xff336699 because offset zero always means the highest byte.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
The final bytes are ff, 66, 33, and 00. The word is 0x003366ff, so red and green remain 51 and 102 while blue becomes 255.

quiz.prompt: What should $t3 contain after this load?

choices.text: The full word 0x003366ff, sign-extended into the register.
Only 0xff because the previous store was a byte store.
The address of pixel rather than its contents.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.
$t3 contains 0x00000000003366ff. Reading the word does not itself draw a new color. The following supplied exit completes the program.

quiz.prompt: Does the same byte offset always identify the same RGB channel in both byte orders?

choices.text: Yes; RGB automatically reverses the address arithmetic.
No; the address-to-byte mapping depends on byte order.
Yes; offset zero always identifies blue.

hints.text: Separate the address, the register value, and the memory bytes in your trace.

A big-endian offset-zero update would produce 0xff336699 while leaving the low-24-bit RGB color unchanged. This is a prediction outside the graded little-endian environment; later byte-order exercises will execute both configurations.
